JSON: Name: slingbag_pipeline Title: Point-cloud-based iterative reconstruction using adaptive Gaussian spherical primitives for large-scale 3D photoacoustic imaging with sparse sensor arrays Short Hypothesis: Modeling a 3D photoacoustic scene as an adaptive point cloud of Gaussian-distributed spherical sources and optimizing their positions, sizes and amplitudes with a differentiable rapid-radiator forward model and adaptive destroy/split/duplicate growth will produce equal-or-better reconstruction fidelity (SSIM and PSNR) than voxel-grid iterative reconstructions and semi-analytical MB-PD methods while using at least an order-of-magnitude less GPU peak memory on large-scale sparse sensor arrays. Related Work: Existing 3D photoacoustic reconstruction approaches fall into several classes: universal back-projection (UBP) and analytic back-projection produce fast reconstructions but generate severe artifacts and low SNR under sparse or limited-view sensor configurations. Voxel-grid model-based iterative reconstruction (time-domain solvers such as k-Wave with LSQR/FISTA) yields higher fidelity but requires explicit volumetric grids, resulting in very large memory and computation costs for large-scale 3D volumes and limits the use of non-smooth regularizers. Semi-analytical model-based point-detector (MB-PD) methods reduce computation by using integral-geometry approximations but rely on far-field/planar assumptions that degrade accuracy near-field or for complex geometries, and they constrain solver choice. Differentiable rendering paradigms (NeRF, 3D Gaussian splatting) show efficient, memory-aware scene representations in vision but have not been adapted to full-wave photoacoustics. Deep-learning methods improve speed or image quality but require large specialized training sets and risk poor generalization across acquisition geometries. Unresolved issues include excessive memory for voxel methods, approximation errors in semi-analytical models in realistic geometries, limited applicability of non-smooth priors in matrix-free solvers, and lack of a differentiable, low-memory forward/backward pipeline tailored to sparse 3D PAI. Abstract: We present a structured pipeline for SlingBAG: a point-cloud-based iterative reconstruction method for large-scale 3D photoacoustic imaging with sparse sensor arrays. The method represents the photoacoustic source distribution as a collection of Gaussian-distributed spherical primitives stored in point-cloud form, and uses a differentiable rapid-radiator forward model that analytically propagates each spherical contribution. During iterative optimization, each primitive’s amplitude, spatial mean and scale are continuously updated and primitives undergo adaptive destroying, splitting and duplication guided by the gradient. The point-cloud-to-voxel shader converts the final primitive set into a conventional 3D voxel volume for analysis and visualization. The pipeline targets scenarios where voxel-grid iterative methods are infeasible due to memory/time constraints and where semi-analytical approximations lose accuracy. Main contributions are: (1) a fully differentiable rapid-radiator forward/backward model for spherical primitives, (2) an adaptive point-cloud growth strategy for automatic complexity control, and (3) a low-memory GPU implementation enabling large-scale 3D reconstructions with sparse sensors. Expected outcomes include comparable or superior image fidelity to grid-based IR at substantially reduced memory usage, enabling practical large-scale 3D photoacoustic reconstruction on commodity GPUs. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Simulated hand vessel volume: physical volume 80 mm × 104 mm × 40 mm, grid spacing 0.2 mm (400×520×200 voxels); ground truth generated analytically; sensor ground truth waveform simulated with k-Wave at 40 MHz, 4900 time samples per channel. (2) Simulated finger phantom: volume 200×520×400 voxels at 0.2 mm spacing; k-Wave ground truth with 4096 temporal samples. (3) In vivo datasets: mouse brain, rat kidney, rat liver acquired with a hemispherical array (1024 elements, radius 60 mm) at 8.33 MHz sampling and 896 time samples; reconstruction grids: mouse 256×256×128 (0.1 mm/pixel), rat volumes 256×256×256 (0.1 mm/pixel). Sensor sparsity configurations: 49, 196, 576, 4900 sensors for planar setups; full 1024 for hemispherical in vivo. Baselines: (A) Universal back-projection (UBP) analytic reconstruction; (B) MB-PD semi-analytical iterative reconstruction with L2 regularization; (C) Voxel-grid full-wave iterative reconstruction using k-Wave forward model with LSQR/FISTA and TV/L2 regularizers (applied when memory allows). Method under test: SlingBAG with specified coarse/fine stages. Evaluation metrics: Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) for top-view MAP and 3D volumes; Mean Squared Error (MSE); Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR, dB); Contrast-to-Noise Ratio (CNR) on MAP; peak amplitude error (relative RMSE on high-intensity voxels); localization error (mm) for identifiable vessel centroids; peak GPU memory consumption (GB); wall-clock reconstruction time (hours) and iterations to convergence. Experimental setup: Run all reconstructions on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 Ti GPU (24 GB) with fixed random seeds; use identical pre-processing (bandpass filtering, time-zero correction) and same voxel grid when applicable. Hyperparameters: report learning rates and stopping criteria; SlingBAG initial point-cloud densities: 600k, 300k, 100k tested. Comparisons: For each dataset and sensor sparsity, compute all metrics for SlingBAG and each baseline. Ablations: (1) SlingBAG without adaptive destroy/split/duplicate (fixed-density point cloud) to test adaptive growth; (2) SlingBAG with spherical discretization orders {4, 6, 10} to test forward-model fidelity vs cost; (3) SlingBAG + explicit regularizers {L1, TV} vs SlingBAG native optimization; (4) sensitivity sweep of learning rates (coarse and fine stage) and initial point-cloud density. Report metric vs sensor count curves, memory/runtime vs method, and statistical summaries (mean±std across 5 random initializations). Risk Factors and Limitations: Modeling and forward-model risks: the differentiable rapid-radiator assumes acoustically homogeneous, non-viscous media and isotropic spherical primitives; departures (spatially varying sound speed, attenuation, anisotropic sources, strong scattering) will bias reconstructions and can invalidate analytic propagation approximations. Near-field and complex boundary geometries may violate semi-analytic assumptions in the discretized spherical approximation, producing localized errors. Optimization risks: convergence depends on learning rates, initialization and scheduler; poor hyperparameter choices can cause slow convergence, trapped local minima, or noisy overfitting to measurement noise. Noise and sensor model mismatch: SlingBAG assumes accurate sensor impulse response and noise statistics; mismatch (unmodeled EIR, correlated noise) will reduce fidelity and may produce spurious primitives. Scalability limits: while point-cloud memory is much lower than dense grids, very fine target resolution or extremely dense initial point sets (multi-million primitives) will increase runtime and may exceed single-GPU compute/time budgets. Generalization limits: performance demonstrated on the tested planar and hemispherical geometries may not directly transfer to radically different array geometries or to strongly heterogeneous biological tissues without model extensions. Evaluation biases: simulated k-Wave ground truth and limited in vivo datasets may underrepresent real acquisition variability; reported superiority may be sensitive to dataset choice and parameter tuning. Regulatory/experimental risks: in vivo studies require adherence to animal protocols and data sharing constraints that may limit reproducibility.
